title: The Most Misunderstood Woman in the Bible
paragraphs:
The Most Misunderstood Woman in the Bible
Mary Magdalene Was Never Who Religion Made Her Become
For centuries, one woman has carried a reputation the Bible itself never gave her.
She has been called a prostitute. A seductress. A fallen woman trying to redeem herself. A symbol of sexual sin.
Entire sermons were built around it. Movies repeated it. Religious tradition reinforced it. Art painted her with shame in her eyes.
But Scripture never says those things.
Not once.
The tragedy is not simply that Mary Magdalene was misunderstood.
The tragedy is that generations of believers repeated something God never said.
And maybe that should terrify us.

Because if humanity can misrepresent one of Jesus Christ’s most faithful followers for centuries, then we should become far more careful with Scripture, tradition, assumptions, and the stories we inherit.
Mary Magdalene is one of the clearest examples of how human tradition can overshadow biblical truth.
Yet when the Greek text is studied carefully, when historical context is restored, and when the Gospel narratives are allowed to speak for themselves, a radically different picture emerges.
Not of a woman defined by immorality.
But of a woman delivered, devoted, courageous, and trusted by Christ Himself.
And perhaps the deeper reason people misunderstand Mary Magdalene is because grace makes religious people uncomfortable.
Especially grace given to women.
Her Name Was Not “Magdalene” Like a Last Name
The Greek text calls her:
Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνή (Maria hē Magdalēnē)
Meaning: “Mary the Magdalene” or “Mary from Magdala.”
Magdala was a town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.
So “Magdalene” was geographical identification. Not moral identification.
She was Mary from Magdala.
This distinction mattered because multiple women in the New Testament were named Mary.
The Hebrew form of Mary is:
מִרְיָם (Miryam)
Which became “Mariam” in Greek.
Mary Magdalene was distinguished by her hometown.
Not by scandal.
The Verse That Started the Misunderstanding
Luke 8:2 says:
“And certain women, which had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities, Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils.”
In Greek:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει
Transliteration: Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē, aph’ hēs daimonia hepta exelēlythei.
Literal meaning: “Mary who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.”
Notice carefully what the text does NOT say.
It does not say she was sexually immoral. It does not say she was a prostitute. It does not say she sold her body. It does not say she committed adultery.
The text only says she had seven demons cast out.
That is all.
Everything else was added later.
Where Did the Prostitute Story Come From?
The misunderstanding largely developed because people merged three different women into one person.
First: The unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7 who anoints Jesus’ feet.
Second: Mary of Bethany, sister of Martha and Lazarus.
Third: Mary Magdalene.
The Bible never identifies these women as the same person.
Yet in 591 AD, Pope Gregory I delivered a sermon that blended these figures together.
From that point forward, Western Christianity increasingly portrayed Mary Magdalene as a repentant prostitute.
But Scripture itself never makes that claim.
Eastern Christianity largely rejected this identification for centuries.
The actual biblical evidence does not support the accusation.
And this matters deeply.
Because when people repeat assumptions long enough, tradition begins to sound like truth.
But tradition is not automatically revelation.
Jesus Himself warned about this.
Mark 7:13 says:
“Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.”
In Greek:
ἀκυροῦντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ παραδόσει ὑμῶν
(akyrountes ton logon tou theou tē paradosei hymōn)
Meaning: “Invalidating the Word of God through your tradition.”
That warning still matters today.
Seven Demons Does Not Automatically Mean Sexual Sin
Modern readers often assume demons in Scripture always symbolize moral perversion.
But the Bible presents demonic oppression in multiple forms.
Some suffered physical torment. Others mental anguish. Others spiritual bondage. Others self-destruction. Others isolation.
The phrase “seven demons” likely emphasizes severity or completeness.
In Hebrew thought, seven often symbolized fullness or totality.
Mary Magdalene may have experienced overwhelming spiritual torment before Christ healed her.
But Scripture never turns her into a sexual sinner.
That distortion says more about human imagination than biblical theology.
And perhaps there is something darker underneath it.
History repeatedly reduces wounded women into moral accusations.
Especially women with complicated pasts.
But Jesus did not define people by the darkness He delivered them from.
He defined them by the transformation that followed.
She Was One of Jesus’ Most Faithful Followers
Luke 8:1-3 reveals something astonishing.
Mary Magdalene financially supported Jesus’ ministry.
The text says:
“And Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward, and Susanna, and many others, which ministered unto him of their substance.”
The Greek word for “ministered” is:
διηκόνουν (diēkonoun)
From:
διακονέω (diakoneō)
Meaning: To serve, support, care for, provide assistance.
This is where the concept of “deacon” originates.
Mary Magdalene was not merely a passive observer.
She was actively supporting the ministry of Jesus Christ.
At a time when women often held little social authority, Christ welcomed women into His ministry circle.
That alone shattered cultural expectations.
Jesus consistently elevated women in ways first-century societies often refused to do.
Not by erasing truth. Not by compromising holiness. But by restoring dignity.
She Stayed When Others Ran
Many disciples fled during the crucifixion.
Fear scattered them.
But Mary Magdalene remained near the cross.
John 19:25 says:
“Now there stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene.”
In Greek:
Εἱστήκεισαν δὲ παρὰ τῷ σταυρῷ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ
(Heistēkeisan de para tō staurō tou Iēsou)
Meaning: “They had taken their stand beside the cross of Jesus.”
That phrase matters.
She stood there.
When Rome displayed public executions. When disciples hid. When crowds mocked. When darkness covered the land. When blood ran down the wood.
She stayed.
The woman religion later shamed was one of the few who remained loyal at Golgotha.
The place called:
Γολγοθᾶ (Golgotha)
From the Aramaic:
גֻּלְגָּלְתָּא (Gulgaltā)
Meaning: “Place of the Skull.”
Mary Magdalene witnessed the horror most others could not endure.
The First Witness of the Resurrection Was a Woman
This is one of the most powerful details in all four Gospels.
In first-century Jewish and Roman culture, women were often not considered reliable legal witnesses.
Yet God chose a woman to first witness the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Not Caesar. Not Pilate. Not the Sanhedrin. Not even Peter first.
Mary Magdalene.
John 20:16 records the resurrected Jesus speaking her name.
“Jesus saith unto her, Mary.”
In Greek:
λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Μαριάμ
(legei autē Iēsous: Mariam)
One word.
Mariam.
And instantly she recognized Him.
The next line says:
“Rabboni.”
In Aramaic:
רַבּוּנִי (Rabbouni)
Meaning: “My Teacher” or “My Master.”
There is breathtaking intimacy in this moment.
Not romantic intimacy.
Spiritual recognition.
The Shepherd called His sheep by name.
And she knew His voice.
“Do Not Cling to Me” Was Deeply Misunderstood Too
Jesus then says:
“Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father.”
John 20:17
In Greek:
Μή μου ἅπτου (Mē mou haptou)
This phrase is often translated awkwardly.
The Greek verb implies: “Stop clinging to Me” or “Do not continue holding onto Me.”
The issue was not that Jesus rejected her.
The moment carries emotional intensity.
Mary Magdalene had lost Him. Then found Him alive. And now Christ was preparing her for a new relationship after resurrection.
Faith would no longer depend upon physical closeness.
The Kingdom was expanding beyond earthly presence.
She Became the Apostle to the Apostles
Early church writers sometimes called Mary Magdalene:
Meaning: “The Apostle to the Apostles.”
Because Jesus sent her to announce the resurrection.
John 20:17:
“Go to my brethren, and say unto them…”
The Greek word:
πορεύου (poreuou)
Meaning: “Go.”
It is a commissioning.
She became the first messenger of the risen Christ.
The first resurrection witness. The first resurrection announcer. The first voice declaring: He is alive.
Yet history remembered her as a prostitute.
That should humble every preacher, teacher, and believer alive.
Because humanity often distorts what God honors.
Why Religious Systems Often Misunderstand Women
Throughout Scripture, women were frequently misjudged.
Hannah was accused of drunkenness.
The woman with the issue of blood was socially isolated.
The Samaritan woman was reduced to her failed relationships.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged publicly while the guilty man vanished.
Even Mary the mother of Jesus faced suspicion surrounding miraculous conception.
Religion often weaponizes shame.
But Jesus exposed hearts.
Not merely behavior.
He saw pain. Trauma. Bondage. Faith. Surrender. Hunger. Repentance.
And He restored people society discarded.
Mary Magdalene became living proof that deliverance does not disqualify someone from devotion.
In fact, sometimes the people most transformed become the most faithful.
Luke 7:47 says:
“For she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.”
Not because grace excuses sin.
But because forgiven people understand mercy differently.
The Dangerous Habit of Adding to Scripture
Revelation 22:18 warns:
“If any man shall add unto these things…”
The warning matters.
Because adding to Scripture is not harmless.
When people invent narratives God never spoke, they can reshape entire generations.
Mary Magdalene carried false labels for centuries.
Some believers still repeat them today without ever reading the text carefully.
This is why studying original languages matters.
Greek. Hebrew. Aramaic.
Not to appear intellectually superior.
But to hear Scripture more clearly.
The Greek text slows us down. It forces us to notice details. It exposes assumptions. It dismantles traditions built on repetition instead of revelation.
And sometimes it restores people history treated unfairly.
What Mary Magdalene Actually Represents
She represents radical deliverance.
She represents loyalty.
She represents courage under pressure.
She represents unwavering devotion to Christ.
She represents transformed identity.
Most importantly:
She represents what happens when Jesus restores a human being society misunderstands.
And perhaps many believers secretly relate to her more than they realize.
Because countless people carry identities God never gave them.
Labels. Rumors. Failures. Mistakes. Assumptions. Past wounds. Old addictions. Broken seasons.
The enemy loves to make people believe their worst chapter became their permanent identity.
But Jesus calls people by name.
Just as He did in the garden.
“Mariam.”
One word changed everything.
The Resurrection Garden Matters More Than We Think
John deliberately places Mary Magdalene in a garden.
That is not accidental.
Humanity fell in a garden.
Now resurrection begins in a garden.
The first Adam brought death. The risen Christ brought life.
Mary Magdalene stands between those realities.
Weeping. Searching. Believing hope was over.
Until Jesus spoke.
And maybe that is where many people are spiritually right now.
Standing in emotional gravesites.
Assuming hope has died.
Not realizing resurrection is already standing beside them.
The Church Must Stop Repeating What the Bible Never Said
This matters beyond historical correction.
It matters spiritually.
Because false narratives damage real people.
Especially women.
When churches casually repeat inaccuracies, they can unknowingly reinforce shame God never assigned.
Truth matters.
Context matters.
Scripture matters.
And humility matters.
The goal of biblical study is not winning arguments.
It is seeing Christ clearly.
Mary Magdalene’s story ultimately points beyond herself.
It points to Jesus.
The Deliverer. The Restorer. The Resurrection.
The Savior who did not erase broken people.
He redeemed them.
The Savior who trusted a formerly tormented woman to carry the greatest announcement in human history:
“He is risen.”
Save this so you never forget the difference between biblical truth and religious tradition.
Some people spent centuries calling her what Jesus never did.
But heaven remembered her as the first witness of the empty tomb.
